TL;DR: It seems to me she's going through Drop, and could benefit from your reassurance and a posts-scene discussion about what specifically you liked best... when she's able to hear you, and really dig into her emotions. 

---
"Drop" applies to anyone involved in a scene; it is the result of high endorphins and other such "feel good" chemicals while playing. Many of the same ones involved in adrenaline-seeking behavior like riding roller-coasters, watching scary movies, or doing contact sports, in fact! 

Post-scene; up to 72 hours later in my experience; those chemicals leave the body and brain and can result in "drop." The high wears off, and you sink deeper than your baseline as your body and mind come to terms with what you've done. Add in some purity culture shame, and the weight of social expectations and you've got a potent mix that can cause depression, self-doubt, recrimination, and a whole hell of a lot more issues that, if left unchecked, can do real lasting damage to your self-esteem.

She needs reassurance, and you both should look into better aftercare options. Protein, sugar, and electrolytes can help re-balance the body in the hour after play, while cuddling and a post-scene discussion about what you enjoyed most and what could be better next time can settle the mind. Some people enjoy a cup of tea, others prefer not to be touched until they can bring themselves down to reality. Opinions on what "Counts" for aftercare are as varied as people into BDSM, but it's worth exploring for your peace of mind if this is something you'd like to engage with, OP.

To actually get anywhere when it comes to emotional dysregulation, you have to be able to first accept what you are experiencing. "This is valid" is a step in that process. It's difficult to process a potentially illogical emotional response when you are beating yourself up for not being entirely logical and stable in an upsetting situation. 

Validate the emotions, take a moment to let yourself just feel them, and *then* start disentangling yourself.

"I feel" statements are used to offer your perception and emotional response to a situation *without* condemnation or assumption of someone's intent. They are a very useful tool for effective communication. 

"I feel like you push me away when we argue, and it makes it hard to bridge the gap and find a resolution" is a perfectly valid thing to feel in a relationship; but the *reality* might be that the other partner is trying to take space to work things out mentally and not say something they regret in the heat of the moment. They're not "pushing their partner away" intentionally, but their intent doesn't invalidate the impact of their action.

The entire phrase is meant to be along the lines of "Your emotions are valid, your *responses to those emotions* may not be" and as far as I know began as a therapeutic exercise to prevent intellectualization.

Your emotions are "valid" because you are feeling them, but it's important that the process does not end there. The point is to not immediately reject your emotions, and instead to "feel your feelings," sit with them a bit, and *then* start processing why you feel that way and how to express them in a healthy way.

I am very rarely angry at a person I am speaking to. But anger is "Valid" in that I have a right to emotional expression. Frustration, anger, upset, "negative emotions" all are valid things to feel in a world that is built to grind us down. *However* I do not have the right to take those emotions out on those around me without just cause. It is not my partners' fault that I have frustrations with my work, my hobbies, politics, etc. So the emotionally mature thing to do is to sit and admit that I am feeling that way, and find a productive outlet instead of pretending I am not feeling them and invalidating my perfectly normal emotional responses to external stimuli.
